title: Development of Religion and Thought in Ancient Egypt
author: James Henry Breasted
location: ch. I, 'The Origins', pp. 8-12, quoting Pyramid Texts §§1248, 1652, 1778, 1818
type: SCHOLARSHIP quoting PRIMARY (Pyramid Texts, c. 2350 BCE)
use: Nun the primeval ocean; Atum appearing in it; the Benben stone and Phoenix-hall at Heliopolis; the self-generation; Shu and Tefnut; Shu separating earth and sky; the rival Memphite egg and lotus versions
scholarship: Breasted is a foundational Egyptologist writing in 1912; his developmental framing of Egyptian religion as progressing toward ethical monotheism is dated and is not adopted here
translation: Breasted's own English from the Egyptian; Pyramid Text section numbers are Sethe's
framing: Nineteenth-century translator reticence: the self-generation is explicit in the Egyptian and Breasted confines it to a Latin footnote. The act is in the source; the veiling is the translator's, and the story says so
uncertainty: The episode of the lost children, the searching eye and the tears is assembled from more than one spell; no single text runs it end to end
notes: Heliopolis, Memphis and Hermopolis each claimed the world began at their temple; the retelling follows Heliopolis and says the others exist

title: Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns and Homerica
author: Hesiod; trans. Hugh G. Evelyn-White
date: composed c. 700 BCE; translation 1914 (Loeb)
location: Theogony ll. 22-34, 116-138, 154-206; Works and Days ll. 106-201
type: PRIMARY / HISTORICAL SOURCE in translation
use: Chaos, Earth, Tartarus and Eros as the first four; Night and Erebos bearing Aether and Day; Earth bearing Ouranos 'equal to herself'; the castration; Aphrodite from the foam; the Muses on Helicon
scholarship: Hesiod is the earliest surviving Greek cosmogony and the earliest Greek text with an autobiographical author
translation: Evelyn-White, Loeb Classical Library 1914, public domain
framing: None colonial. The translator's 'Chaos' imports a modern English sense the Greek does not carry
uncertainty: Hesiod's own etymologies (Titans as 'straining ones', Aphrodite as 'foam-born') are folk etymologies rejected by modern philology; the story reports them as his
notes: The one text in this book whose author describes his own life

title: Indian Myth and Legend
author: Donald A. Mackenzie
location: ch. VI, pp. 99-101
type: SCHOLARSHIP quoting PRIMARY (Brāhmaṇa texts, c. 900-600 BCE)
use: 'At first the Universe was not anything... Being non-existent it resolved, Let me be'; the heat/smoke/fire/rays/sea sequence; Prajāpati rising from the waters and weeping; earth, air and sky from tears and wiping; the rodasī etymology
scholarship: Mackenzie is a popular compiler, not a Sanskritist; this entry therefore works at one remove and is marked PRIMARY-QUOTED-IN-SECONDARY
translation: Mackenzie quotes an unattributed nineteenth-century English translation; the underlying text is Brāhmaṇa material
framing: Mackenzie writes within an Indo-European comparative framework of his period; that framing is not adopted
uncertainty: HIGH on the translation chain. The quoted English cannot be traced to a named translator in the source
notes: Ṛgveda 10.129, the Nāsadīya Sūkta, was originally to be named and not quoted because no public-domain English Mandala 10 could be found (correction C-1). Griffith's volume IV was subsequently located and the hymn is now quoted in full from it — see the second source record for this story

title: The Hymns of the Rigveda, volume IV (Books IX and X)
author: trans. Ralph T. H. Griffith
date: hymn composed in the late Vedic period; Griffith's four-volume translation published 1889-1892
location: Book X, hymn CXXIX ('Creation'), verses 1-7, with Griffith's notes
type: PRIMARY / HISTORICAL SOURCE in translation
use: the Nāsadīya Sūkta quoted in full at the close of the story: neither non-existent nor existent; no realm of air; the unfathomed water; no death and nothing immortal; That One Thing breathing breathlessly; darkness in darkness; tapas; desire as the primal seed; the line drawn across; the gods being later than the world's production; and the final 'he verily knows it, or perhaps he knows not'
scholarship: Griffith glosses asat as that which does not yet actually exist but holds the latent potentiality of existence, and quotes an Indian commentator on the 'unapparent condition' that was neither entity nor non-entity. He notes that Wilson, following Sāyaṇa, renders tapas as 'austerity', and that Burnouf treated warmth as the Vedic principle of movement, life and thought
translation: Griffith's English verse from the Sanskrit
framing: A Victorian Indologist's translation, made in Benares, heavily annotated from Sāyaṇa's commentary. Griffith's diction is archaic; his notes are cautious and he marks the stanzas he finds obscure as obscure
uncertainty: LOW on the English quoted. The Sanskrit of verse 5 is notoriously difficult and Griffith says so; the retelling summarises that verse rather than quoting it
notes: THE SCAN HAS NO TITLE PAGE — it begins mid-Book IX. Identity established from content and recorded in the source register. The citation names the translator and volume and does not assert a printing year the file cannot support

title: Pahlavi Texts, Part I (Sacred Books of the East, vol. V)
author: trans. E. W. West
date: Bundahishn compiled 9th c. CE from older Avestan material; translation 1880
location: Bundahishn I.1-11; Selections of Zādsparam I.1-8; West's introduction pp. xxiii-xxv
type: PRIMARY / HISTORICAL SOURCE in translation
use: Light above, darkness below, void between; Ohrmazd omniscient, Ahriman ignorant of him; 3,000 years of spiritual creation with intangible bodies; Ahriman seeing a ray of light; the Ahunwar driving him back; the 9,000-year contract; the six creations and the damage to each
scholarship: West's SBE translation remains the standard PD English Bundahishn
translation: West 1880, from the Pahlavi
framing: Nineteenth-century Orientalist scholarship; West is philologically careful and doctrinally restrained
uncertainty: The Bundahishn is fragmentary and shows omissions and dislocations, which West states
notes: Zoroastrianism is a living faith with a small community; the story treats the cosmology as held now, not as a Sasanian curiosity. West's Auharmazd/Aharman are modernised to Ohrmazd/Ahriman in the prose and the change is disclosed

title: Oceanic Mythology (The Mythology of All Races, vol. IX)
author: Roland B. Dixon
location: ch. I, 'Myths of Origins and the Deluge', pp. 6-7
type: SCHOLARSHIP quoting a recorded PRIMARY genealogy
use: The nine Te Kore and the nights with their English glosses; Whai-tua; Maku and Mahora-nui-a-rangi; Rangi-pōtiki and Papa; the 'From the conception the increase' recitation
scholarship: Dixon is a comparative mythologist working from other men's collections; he does not name the New Zealand informant for this list
translation: Glosses are those Dixon's source supplies
framing: Comparative-mythology framing of 1916, which classes accounts by type; the classification is not adopted
uncertainty: 'The Delightful Void' for Te Kore-rawea is unexplained in the source; the story offers a speculation and marks it as one
notes: Macrons follow modern Māori orthography except where a source spelling is quoted

title: Polynesian Mythology and Ancient Traditional History of the New Zealand Race
author: Sir George Grey
location: 'The Children of Heaven and Earth', opening
type: PRIMARY / HISTORICAL SOURCE (colonial compilation from named Māori informants)
use: 'There was darkness from the first division of time, unto the tenth, to the hundredth, to the thousandth'; the divisions of time considered as beings, each termed a Pō; 'Darkness, darkness, light, light, the seeking, the searching, in chaos, in chaos'
scholarship: Grey's versions have been contested by Māori scholars for a century and a half for editorial combination
translation: Grey's English from Māori originals he also published
framing: NAMED IN THE STORY: Grey was the sitting Governor of New Zealand during a colonial administration in which he was a principal actor, and he collected these narratives from named informants while holding that office
uncertainty: Grey edited and combined what he was given; the degree is disputed
notes: The separation of Rangi and Papa is deliberately NOT retold — Agent C published it for young readers

title: The Chaldean Account of Genesis
author: George Smith; new edition revised, corrected and enlarged by A. H. Sayce
date: first published London 1876; this edition New York: Charles Scribner's Sons, 1880 (Sayce's preface dated 21 May 1880)
location: ch. V 'Babylonian Legend of the Creation' (first tablet, fifth tablet, seventh tablet fragment); ch. VI 'Other Babylonian Accounts of the Creation' (the war fragments K 4832, K 3473, K 3938, K 3449 and the sixth fragment); ch. III (Berosus via Alexander Polyhistor; Damascius via Cory); ch. I (the discovery narrative); ch. IV (the table of deities)
type: PRIMARY / HISTORICAL SOURCE in translation (cuneiform tablets), embedded in nineteenth-century SCHOLARSHIP
use: the unnamed heaven and earth; destiny not fixed; Apsu as generator and Tiamat as she who bore them; waters collected in one place; the ungathered reed and ungrown marsh-plant; Lakhmu and Lakhamu, Sar and Kisar, Anu, Elum and Hea; the colophon of Assurbanipal; the making of the scimitar and Anu kissing the bow; the winds; Tiamat's spells and her determined return; the evil wind in her mouth and her death; the rout of her helpers; Kingu named; Berosus on Omoroka cut asunder and on the blood mixed with earth; the fifth tablet in full (mansions, zodiac, Nibiru, gates and bolts, staircase, the moon's instructions, 'judge judgment'); the four-line animal fragment
scholarship: Smith is the decipherer who found these tablets; his translations are careful and his statements of uncertainty are explicit. Sayce's 1880 revision adds material and corrects readings. Both write inside a Victorian biblical-comparative programme announced by the book's own title
translation: Smith's and Sayce's English direct from the Assyrian cuneiform; the Berosus and Damascius extracts are Smith's reprints of I. P. Cory's English of the Greek
framing: NAMED IN THE STORY AND IN THE HISTORICAL CONTEXT: the volume is titled *The Chaldean Account of Genesis* and arranges the fragments against the six days of Genesis 1. The philology (tehom / Tiamat) is sound; the frame treats a Babylonian poem as an account of a Hebrew one. This edition keeps the translations and drops the frame
uncertainty: HIGH on sequence, LOW on wording. Smith states that the order of the war fragments cannot be decided and that one 'dry land' fragment probably does not belong to the series at all. Three tablets between the first and the fifth were entirely missing to him. The retelling marks the break rather than bridging it
notes: Later editions recovered much more of the poem — the standard next edition is L. W. King, *The Seven Tablets of Creation* (London, 1902). NONE of that material has been used here. Where Smith's clay stops, the retelling changes witness to Berosus openly. Spellings modernised outside quotations; disclosed in the source note
workAuthor: George Smith; rev. A. H. Sayce

title: Iroquoian Cosmology, First Part — An Onondaga Version
author: narrated by John Buck (Onondaga chief and fire-keeper), revised with Joshua Buck; recorded, translated and annotated by J. N. B. Hewitt
date: narrated 1889, revised 1897; published in the Twenty-first Annual Report of the Bureau of American Ethnology (Washington: Government Printing Office)
location: report pp. 141 ff. ('An Onondaga version'), with Hewitt's introduction pp. 127-135; comparative details from 'A Seneca version' (p. 221 ff.) and 'A Mohawk version' (p. 255 ff.)
type: PRIMARY / HISTORICAL SOURCE AS RECORDED (a named Onondaga narrator, in Onondaga, with interlinear and free English translation), embedded in United States federal SCHOLARSHIP
use: the grandfather's five generations; the sky world and its long lodges; the two down-fended persons and the combing; the unexplained pregnancy; the first illness and the first death; the burial case in the high place; the child who wept five days; the armlet and the necklace; the father's instructions; the bread and the burden basket; Aurora Borealis, Fire Dragon of the Storm and the chief at the crossing; the tree called Tooth and its blossoms as the light; 'Thou and I marry'; the mush ordeal, the two white dogs and the sunflower oil; the basket shaken seven times; the unroofed lodges and the raining corn; the breath caught in conversation and the origin of reproduction; the chief's illness and jealousy; the naming of Zephyrs; the dream feast and the list of those who came to divine the Word; Aurora Borealis divining it; the uprooting of the tree and the abyss; the fawn meat and the three fagots; the push; the blue light, the lake and the ducks; the Loon and the Bittern; the Otter sinking and the Turtle holding; the Muskrat surfacing dead with earth in his paws and mouth; the growing carapace; the waterfowl joining their bodies to catch her; the first fire, the deer, and the second birth of Zephyrs
scholarship: Hewitt's method — verbatim recording in the vernacular with literal interlinear gloss plus free translation, named narrators, dated and located sessions — is unusually rigorous for its period and is the reason the text remains usable
translation: Hewitt's English from Onondaga, printed beneath his own interlinear literal gloss
framing: NAMED IN THE HISTORICAL CONTEXT: a Bureau of American Ethnology publication of the assimilation era, written inside a cultural-evolutionary theory whose vocabulary ('primitive people', 'barbaric man', 'the reified fictions of savage mentation') appears throughout Hewitt's commentary and nowhere in the narratives themselves. Hewitt was raised on the Tuscarora reservation and was of Tuscarora descent through his mother, which does not make the report a Haudenosaunee publication
uncertainty: LOW on wording, once the clean scan is used. The three versions in the report differ substantially from one another and the retelling follows one of them throughout, saying so and listing the divergences rather than blending them
notes: Hewitt records a fourth, fuller Onondaga version from Chief John Arthur Gibson, promised for a later report and not present in this one. The retelling stops at the growing earth and the second birth of Zephyrs; the cycle of the twin brothers Sapling and Flint that follows in the source is not told here, both because this is a book of cosmogonies and because DC-11 reserves hero cycles to the Codex Heroica series

title: Myths of the Cherokee
author: collected, translated and annotated by James Mooney, from narrators named in his introduction: A'yûñ'ini (Swimmer), Itagû'nahi (John Ax), Ta'gwadihi' (Catawba-killer), Ayâ'sta, and James D. Wafford
date: collected 1887-1890 and later at Qualla, North Carolina; published in the Nineteenth Annual Report of the Bureau of American Ethnology (Washington: Government Printing Office, 1900)
location: myth no. 1, 'How the world was made', p. 239; Mooney's note on myth 1 in 'Notes to the myths', p. 431; the biographies of the narrators, pp. 236-238; the removal narrative in the historical sketch, pp. 130-133
type: PRIMARY / HISTORICAL SOURCE AS RECORDED (named Cherokee narrators), embedded in United States federal SCHOLARSHIP
use: the earth as an island slung from the sky vault by four cords and the fear of the cords breaking; the crowding in Galûñ'lati; Dâyuni'si the water-beetle and the soft mud; the four cords fastened by no one remembered; the birds sent to test the ground; the Great Buzzard and the making of the Cherokee mountains; the sun raised seven hand-breadths and Tsiska'gili' the Red Crawfish; the seventh height; the underworld with reversed seasons reached by springs; the seven nights of watching, the owl and panther, the evergreens and the losing of hair; the brother, the sister and the fish; one child a year
scholarship: Mooney's note on this myth states that the Cherokee genesis account is 'too far broken down to be recovered excepting in disjointed fragments' through decay of tradition and admixture of Bible ideas, and identifies which narrator supplied which element. His comparative notes point to Creek and Yuchi parallels and identify the beetle as the Gyrinus
translation: Mooney's English from Cherokee
framing: NAMED IN THE HISTORICAL CONTEXT: a Bureau of American Ethnology publication written on the salvage assumption that Cherokee tradition was in its final days, and measuring what Mooney recorded against a supposed complete original. Against that, the same volume records the removal of 1838 as an atrocity, in a report addressed to the government responsible for it
uncertainty: MEDIUM on the completeness of the account, by the collector's own statement. LOW on wording. The printed myth is a composite of at least four narrators and Mooney's note says so; the variants are listed in the source note rather than merged
notes: Swimmer supplied roughly three-quarters of the whole collection and died in March 1899, before publication. This retelling does not use Mooney's myth no. 2 ('The first fire') or any other numbered myth

title: Kalevala: The Epic Poem of Finland
author: compiled by Elias Lönnrot from oral runes collected in Savo, Karelia and Archangel; translated into English verse by John Martin Crawford
date: runes collected from 1828; Old Kalevala 1835; New Kalevala (50 runes, 22,793 lines) 1849; Crawford's translation New York, 1888
location: Rune I, 'Birth of Wainamoinen', in full; the Proem for the clasped-hands couplet; Crawford's preface for the collection history, the duck/eagle variant, the reception by Grimm and others, and his own acknowledgements
type: PRIMARY / HISTORICAL SOURCE in translation — but of a NINETEENTH-CENTURY COMPILATION, not of a single old text
use: the singer's call to a second singer and the clasped hands; Ilmatar alone in the ether and her weariness; her descent to the sea; the east wind, the tossing and the conception; seven hundred years and nine ages of man; her lament and her prayer to Ukko; Ukko's silence; the duck's search and its spoken reasoning; the raised knee mistaken for a hillock; six golden eggs and one of iron; three days' brooding and the burning knee; the shaken nest and the shattered eggs; the fragments becoming earth, sky, moon, sun, stars and cloud; the ninth year and the making of headlands, fish-holes, deeps, banks, bays, rocks and the wrecking reefs; Väinämöinen's thirty summers and thirty winters unborn; his petition to Moon, Sun and Great Bear and their refusal; the unnamed finger, the left toes, the threshold; seven further years in the sea; the bare promontory and standing up to look at the stars
scholarship: Crawford's preface is the source for the collection history and is detailed and specific. The Kalevala's status as a compiled national epic is not a modern criticism of it — it is stated by its own translator
translation: Crawford's English verse in the original trochaic metre. His acknowledgements record that his manuscript was compared against Schiefner's German translation and Barna's Hungarian; how directly he worked from the Finnish has been questioned since
framing: NAMED IN THE HISTORICAL CONTEXT: a work of nineteenth-century cultural nationalism, produced under Russian imperial rule for a Finnish-speaking population whose language had almost no printed literature. Lönnrot arranged the collected songs 'under the central idea of a great epic'. Crawford's own account of Finland's political status in the 1820s is wrong and is corrected in the historical context
uncertainty: HIGH on the relation of any given line to any individual singer's version — the text is Lönnrot's arrangement. LOW on the wording of Crawford's English, which is what is quoted
notes: Rune I is used alone. Rune II (Väinämöinen's sowing) and the rest of the epic, including the Sampo and the Kullervo cycle, are not told here — DC-11 reserves hero cycles to the Codex Heroica series, and DC-12 records the Kalevala as a Vâliçe public-domain reserve title, which this book cites and does not reproduce
workAuthor: comp. Elias Lönnrot; trans. John Martin Crawford

title: The Ainu and their Folk-Lore
author: John Batchelor, F.R.G.S., Church Missionary Society missionary to the Ainu
date: London: The Religious Tract Society, 1901
location: ch. III, 'The Creation of the World' — the general idea of creation; the water-wagtail legends; the legend why Yezo is rugged; the Aioina and Tureshmat variant and the nupe etymology; the axe rock at Moruran; 'How mattocks evolved demons' and Nitat-unarabe
type: HISTORICAL SOURCE — MISSIONARY ETHNOGRAPHY recording Ainu oral tradition; narrators unnamed
use: the quagmire of mixed earth and water incapable of sustaining life; the thunder demons and the Creator's subordinate deities; the wagtail sent down; the fluttering, trampling and tail-beating; moshiri, floating earth; the wagtail as the angel of God; the second version with God's mattocks and axes and the wagtail levelling; 'God is never conceived of as working without means'; the sixty mattocks decomposing into demons, bad water and disease-bearing trees; Nitat-unarabe, aunt of the swamps, and the Toihekunra; the two deputy deities and the race to finish Yezo; the chat with Aioina's sister and the botched west coast; the moral quoted at talkative women; Tureshmat's weeping and the nupe wordplay; mukara-so, axe rock
scholarship: Batchelor lived among Ainu for decades and compiled an Ainu-English-Japanese dictionary. His own commentary on this chapter is hostile to its contents and is quoted rather than used
translation: Batchelor's English from Ainu
framing: NAMED IN THE STORY AND THE SOURCE NOTE: a Church Missionary Society missionary writing for the Religious Tract Society, who introduces the chapter by calling much of the material 'absolutely absurd' and an illustration of 'what depths of intellectual blindness a race may sink into'. He also floats and then rejects the idea that the wagtail legend derives from Genesis 1
uncertainty: HIGH on attribution — no narrator is named anywhere in the chapter, and the one identified informant is 'an Ainu companion' on a walk. MEDIUM on completeness, since Batchelor selects. LOW on the wording quoted, which was checked against the scan
notes: OCR of the available scan is imperfect; quotations verified line by line. Yezo is the pre-1869 name for Hokkaidō. The retelling attributes to Batchelor's book, never to a named Ainu person, because the book supplies no names. Under the academic source and historical document model this book does not present the material as current Ainu belief

title: The Mahabharata of Krishna-Dwaipayana Vyasa, Translated into English Prose — Book 1, Adi Parva
author: traditionally ascribed to Vyāsa; translated by Kisari Mohan Ganguli, with acknowledged assistance from Charu Charan Mookerjee in parts of this book; published by Pratap Chandra Roy
date: epic material accreted over centuries around the turn of the era; translation published in fascicles, Calcutta, 1883-1896
location: Āstīka Parva, sections XVII, XVIII and XIX; the Translator's Preface for the method and the anonymity dispute
type: PRIMARY / HISTORICAL SOURCE in translation
use: Nārāyaṇa's instruction to churn the Ocean for amṛta, drugs and gems; Meru and the assembled celestials; Mandara eleven thousand yojanas up and down; the gods' failure to lift it and Ananta tearing it up with woods and inhabitants; the request to the Ocean and its condition of a share; the tortoise-king's back; Vasuki as rope with Asuras at the hood and gods at the tail; the black vapour, flames, thunderclouds and refreshing rain; the flowers; the roar as at the Universal Dissolution; the crushed aquatic animals, the killed denizens of the lower regions, the uprooted trees with birds, the friction fires and the burned lions and elephants; Indra's rain; the gums and juices conferring immortality; the milky water turning to clarified butter; 'we are spent up'; the emergence in order of Moon, Lakṣmī, Soma, the White Steed, Kaustubha, Dhanvantari with the white vessel, and Airāvata; 'It be ours'; Kālakūṭa engulfing the earth and stupefying the three worlds; Śiva holding it in his throat and becoming Nīlakaṇṭha; the Asuras arming for Lakṣmī and amṛta; Nārāyaṇa's māyā and the enticing female form; Rāhu drinking in disguise; Sūrya and Soma informing; the discus and the head cut off at the throat; the head rising and crying, the trunk shaking the earth; the eclipses
scholarship: Ganguli's is the first complete English Mahābhārata and remains the standard public-domain one. His preface states an explicitly literal method and rejects making Indian ideas 'agreeable to English taste'
translation: Ganguli's English prose direct from the Sanskrit
framing: Not colonial in the usual sense of this book: an Indian translation, Indian-financed, Calcutta-printed, deliberately literal in resistance to the domesticating translations of the period. The anonymity dispute recorded in the preface is itself a document of what English readers of 1885 expected
uncertainty: LOW on wording. The epic is a composite text of uncertain and layered date, which is stated in the historical context rather than smoothed over
notes: The battle of the gods and Asuras that follows section XIX is deliberately not retold — DC-11 reserves hero cycles to the Codex Heroica series, and this is a book of origins. This is the second Indian entry and is kept distinct in period and literature from S03

title: The Elder Eddas of Saemund Sigfusson (Poetic Edda)
author: anonymous Old Norse poems; trans. Benjamin Thorpe
date: poems of uncertain and disputed age, preserved chiefly in the Codex Regius of c. 1270; Thorpe's translation 1866, in the Norrœna Society edition edited by Rasmus B. Anderson
location: Vǫluspá 3-6; Vafþrúðnismál 20-21, 29-35; Grímnismál 40-41; Vǫluspá 9-10, 17-18
type: PRIMARY / HISTORICAL SOURCE in translation
use: the chasm with neither sand nor sea nor grass; Ymir's flesh, bones, skull and blood becoming earth, hills, heaven and sea; the venom drops from Élivágar and the sparks from the south-world; Bergelmir born countless winters before the earth and laid in an ark; Aurgelmir's self-generation under the armpit and foot on foot; the fuller Grímnismál inventory adding hair as trees and plants, brows as Midgard, brain as clouds; the sun, moon and stars not knowing their places; the council naming night, morning, midday, afternoon and evening so that years could be reckoned; the gods in council deciding who should create the race of dwarfs from the sea-giant's blood and bones; Móðsognir and Durin; Ask and Embla found nearly powerless and void of destiny; the gifts of spirit, sense, blood and goodly colour from Óðinn, Hœnir and Lóðurr
scholarship: The poems are the oldest witnesses; Snorri quotes them and the retelling follows them where the two differ
translation: Thorpe's English from the Old Norse. The file is Project Gutenberg #14726, whose title page credits Thorpe for the Elder Edda and I. A. Blackwell for the Younger
framing: Nineteenth-century Northern antiquarianism, issued as a subscription set. The translations themselves are literal and unembellished
uncertainty: HIGH on the age of the poems, which is disputed and not settled here. LOW on the English quoted
notes: THE FILE IS NAMED FOR BELLOWS AND IS NOT BELLOWS — correction C-2. Identity established from the title page inside the file

title: The Younger Edda; also called Snorre's Edda, or The Prose Edda
author: Snorri Sturluson; trans. Rasmus B. Anderson
date: composed in Iceland in the 1220s; Anderson's translation copyrighted 1879, this printing Chicago: Scott, Foresman, 1901
location: Gylfaginning, sections 5-8; Gylfaginning 9 and 14
type: PRIMARY / HISTORICAL SOURCE in translation
use: Niflheim's ice and rime and Muspelheim's sparks; Ginnungagap warm and mild as windless air; the meltwater quickening into Ymir; the denial that Ymir is a god and the statement that he and his offspring were evil; the sweat, the armpit and the foot; Auðhumla and the four milk-streams; the licking of the salt-stones over three days producing hair, head and whole man; Búri, Borr, Bestla and the three sons; the killing of Ymir; the blood drowning all the frost-giants but Bergelmir in his ark; the dismemberment inventory; the ocean laid in a ring; the skull raised with four corners and a dwarf under each, named for the four directions; the sparks from Muspelheim fixed as lights with assigned courses; the dwarfs quickening in Ymir's flesh like maggots and being given understanding and the likeness of men while remaining in earth and rock; Borr's sons finding two trees on the sea-strand and making Ask and Embla, with the three gifts and the giving of clothes and names
scholarship: The Gylfaginning is a poet's handbook, not a scripture, and strings verse citations together with explanatory prose. Where Snorri supplies what no surviving poem contains, the material may come from a lost poem or from Snorri
translation: Anderson's English from the Old Norse
framing: NAMED IN THE HISTORICAL CONTEXT: a Christian Icelandic author writing two centuries after the conversion, who in his preface explains the gods as misremembered human beings and ends the dialogue by revealing the whole vision as an illusion
uncertainty: MEDIUM on details unique to Snorri — the cow, the salt-stones, the three days, the four dwarfs — which cannot be checked against a surviving poem
notes: THE FILE IS NAMED FOR BRODEUR AND IS NOT BRODEUR — correction C-6. Identified from the title page and confirmed by Anderson's distinctive spellings
workAuthor: Snorri Sturluson; trans. Rasmus B. Anderson

title: Myths and Legends of China
author: E. T. C. Werner
date: London: George G. Harrap, 1922
location: ch. III, 'Cosmogony — P'an Ku and the Creation Myth': the fashioner of the universe; the sun and the moon; P'an Ku and Ymer; P'an Ku a late creation; Nue Kua Shih the repairer of the heavens
type: SCHOLARSHIP SUMMARISING A TRADITION — not a primary text and not a primary text quoted; see correction C-7
use: Pangu as offspring of yin and yang set to give form to Chaos; the name elements 'shell of an egg' and 'to secure'; the bearskin, the leaves, the two horns, the hammer and chisel; the four supernatural creatures; the sun and moon in his hands; eighteen thousand years and six feet of growth a day; 'he died that his works might live'; the full transformation inventory from head to sweat; the insects becoming human beings and Werner's comparison to the tears of Khepera; the Taoist origin of the account and the later Buddhist adaptation; the sun and moon hiding in the Han Sea, Terrestrial Time, Ju Lai, the characters written on the palms and the charm said seven times; the dragon-headed and serpent-bodied variant and the breathing, eye-opening, thunder-voiced variant; Werner's attribution of the myth's invention to Ko Hung in the fourth century and his argument that the classical cosmogonies were impersonal; Nüwa the repairer, quoted by Werner from Sima Zhen
scholarship: Werner was a British consular official in China for more than thirty years. He distinguishes Taoist from Buddhist versions, marks late adaptations, and reports variants rather than harmonising them
translation: Werner's own English; no Chinese text is quoted in the Pangu section
framing: NAMED IN THE SOURCE NOTE: the confident comparative manner of 1922, including appeals to a national temperament ('the ordinary mind', 'the placid Chinese mind') and a diffusionist speculation about the Chinese bringing a cosmogony from Babylon. Neither assumption is adopted here
uncertainty: HIGH on wording — there is no primary text behind Werner's Pangu paragraphs that this book can check. MEDIUM on his dating and attribution, corrected in the historical context
notes: Werner independently compares Pangu with Ymir and adapts a stanza of the Vǫluspá to do it — the same poem used in the preceding story. DC-12 records Werner as a Vâliçe public-domain reserve title: this book cites it and does not reproduce it

title: The Hymns of the Rigveda, volume IV (Books IX and X)
author: anonymous Vedic poets, the hymn ascribed by tradition to the ṛṣi Nārāyaṇa; trans. Ralph T. H. Griffith
date: hymn composed in the latest stratum of the Ṛgveda; Griffith's four-volume translation published 1889-1892
location: Book X, hymn XC, verses 1-16, with Griffith's notes and his closing bibliographic note
type: PRIMARY / HISTORICAL SOURCE in translation
use: the thousand heads, eyes and feet; covering the earth and extending ten fingers' breadth beyond; all that has been and is to be; the lord of immortality; the one-fourth of created things and three-fourths in heaven; striding over what eats not and what eats; Virāj born from Puruṣa and Puruṣa from Virāj; the sacrifice with spring as its oil, autumn as the gift, summer as the wood; the anointing on the grass and the participation of gods, Sādhyas and ṛṣis; the dripping fat producing birds and animals; the Ṛcas, Sāman, metres and Yajus; horses, two-rowed-teeth animals, cattle, goats and sheep; the question of the portions; the Brahman from the mouth, Rājanya from the arms, Vaiśya from the thighs, Śūdra from the feet; moon from mind, sun from eye, Indra and Agni from the mouth, Vāyu from the breath; mid-air from the navel, sky from the head, earth from the feet, the regions from the ear; the seven fencing-logs and thrice seven layers of fuel; and the closing line on the earliest holy ordinances
scholarship: Griffith notes that this is the only passage in the Ṛgveda enumerating the four castes, and that the hymn is of comparatively recent origin and appears to harmonise the ideas of sacrifice and creation. His notes print competing renderings — Wilson, Sāyaṇa, Colebrooke, Muir, Ludwig, Peterson, the Bhāgavata Purāṇa — without choosing between them
translation: Griffith's English verse from the Sanskrit, made in Benares with Sāyaṇa's commentary
framing: NAMED IN THE SOURCE NOTE: Griffith's gloss explaining why each caste derives from its body part — the labourer from the feet because on his toil all ultimately rests — is a Victorian interpretation, not a translation, and is quoted as his without agreement
uncertainty: LOW on the English quoted. Verse 5 (Virāj) is genuinely disputed and Griffith prints two readings; the retelling reports both and settles neither
notes: THE SCAN HAS NO TITLE PAGE — identity established from content and recorded in the source register. The same volume supplies the Nāsadīya Sūkta quoted at the close of S03. This is the third Indian entry and is kept distinct in stratum and literature from S03 (Brāhmaṇa prose) and S11 (epic)

title: Pahlavi Texts, Part I (Sacred Books of the East, vol. V)
author: trans. E. W. West
date: Bundahishn compiled 9th c. CE from older Avestan material; translation 1880
location: Bundahishn IV.1-5 (the two deaths and the complaint of Gōshurvan); X.1-4 and XIV.1-5 (what grew from the ox and from its seed); XV.1-13 (the rhubarb plant, Mashya and Mashyoi, the soul-and-body question, Ohrmazd's charge, the false speeches, the goat); Selections of Zādsparam X.2-4 (the eight metals and Spandarmad receiving the gold)
type: PRIMARY / HISTORICAL SOURCE in translation

scholarship: West notes that the complaint of Gōshurvan is recorded in the Gāthās, the oldest part of the Avesta, at Yasna 29; that the animal's gender is doubtful in the Avesta and treated as female by Zādsparam; and that the rivās is a rhubarb-like plant whose acid juice the Persians used for preserves and drinks. He records manuscript variants in every figure
translation: West's English from the Pahlavi
framing: Nineteenth-century Orientalist scholarship, philologically careful and doctrinally restrained; the frame was set out in full at the earlier Iranian story and is not restated
uncertainty: MEDIUM on the numbers, which differ between manuscripts and are given here in the majority reading with the variants recorded. MEDIUM on the ox's gender. LOW on the wording quoted
notes: Second Zoroastrian entry. As with the first, this is a living religion; the material is presented as what the ninth-century compilation records in an 1880 translation, and nobody Zoroastrian has reviewed it. West's transliteration characters are rendered unreliably by the available scan, which is a further reason the retelling paraphrases where it does not quote

title: Latin-American Mythology (The Mythology of All Races, vol. XI)
author: Hartley Burr Alexander, drawing on the *Historia de los Mexicanos por sus pinturas*, Ixtlilxochitl, the *Annals of Quauhtitlan*, the *Codex Vaticanus A*, Camargo and Sahagún
date: Boston: Marshall Jones, 1920; the underlying documents are sixteenth-century
location: ch. III, 'Mexico (Continued)', section I 'Cosmogony' and section II 'The Four Suns'
type: SCHOLARSHIP reporting sixteenth-century colonial documents which themselves record pre-conquest tradition
use: Tonacatecuhtli and Tonacacihuatl in the thirteenth heaven; the four sons — red Camaxtli, black Tezcatlipoca, Quetzalcoatl the wind, Huitzilopochtli born a skeleton; six hundred years of idleness with time uncounted while Huitzilopochtli was in his bones; the making of fire first and then a half-sun; Oxomoco and Cipactonal and their allotted work, with divination and curing maize given to the woman; the year of eighteen twenty-day periods; Mictlantecuhtli and Mictlancihuatl; the heavens below the thirteenth; the sea and the monster Cipactli from which the earth was shaped; Tlaloc and Chalchiuhtlicue over the Quarters; the wife made from a hair of Xochiquetzal; the second half-sun and Tezcatlipoca as sun-bearer; the true sun being invisible; the giants who uprooted trees and ate acorns; the four Suns with their lengths of 676, 676, 364 and 312 years; Tezcatlipoca cast down and becoming the jaguar of Ursa Major who devoured the giants; Quetzalcoatl treated by his brothers as he had treated Tezcatlipoca; the wind and the monkeys; the rain of fire; maize first used under Chalchiuhtlicue; the year 2,628 and the falling heavens and the people turned to fish; the four men and the re-raising of the sky by Tezcatlipoca and Quetzalcoatl; fire discovered from sticks and from the heart of flint; Piltzintecuhtli and his wife surviving because divine; Quetzalcoatl casting his son into the fire to make the Sun and Tlaloc casting his into the cinders to make the Moon; and the establishment of war so that the Sun might be fed with hearts and blood
scholarship: Alexander sets five incompatible orderings of the Suns side by side and states that no single account preserves the whole. His own proposal that the whole 'may be reasonably reconstructed' is a scholarly act and is not followed here
translation: Alexander's English, working from Spanish and Nahuatl documents and from earlier scholarship; he quotes Herrera and Fray Gregorio García directly elsewhere in the chapter
framing: NAMED IN THE HISTORICAL CONTEXT: every underlying document is post-conquest, most produced by or for the colonial church and administration, after the systematic burning of the Mexica painted books. Alexander adds his own comparative identifications, of which only those present in his sources are used
uncertainty: HIGH on the sequence of the Suns, which the sources contradict each other about; the retelling follows one document throughout and prints the disagreement. MEDIUM on names, because the available scan's optical character recognition is poor and each proper name was checked against its least corrupted occurrence
notes: THE PLANNED STORY WAS NOT IN THE SOURCE — correction C-8. The Tlaltecuhtli dismemberment is absent from Alexander and its usual source, the Histoyre du Mechique, could not be obtained in public-domain English. S16 re-scoped and re-titled rather than written from memory

title: Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697
author: compiled by imperial order, traditionally under Prince Toneri and Ō no Yasumaro; trans. W. G. Aston
date: chronicle completed 720; Aston's translation published for the Japan Society, London, 1896
location: Book I, 'The Age of the Gods', opening pages: the egg and the separation; the reed-shoot and Kuni-toko-tachi; the five 'In one writing it is said' variants; the seven generations; the jewel-spear and Onogoro; the circling of the pillar; the birth of the islands. Aston's footnotes on Motoori and Hirata, on the later addition of the variant quotations, on the Kiujiki scheme, and on the name etymologies
type: PRIMARY / HISTORICAL SOURCE in translation
use: heaven and earth unseparated, In and Yō undivided, a chaotic mass like an egg with obscurely defined limits containing germs; the purer part drawn out as Heaven and the grosser settling as Earth; the finer uniting easily and the gross consolidating with difficulty; heaven formed first; the soil floating like a fish sporting on the surface; the reed-shoot between heaven and earth becoming Kuni-toko-tachi; the five variant beginnings including the thing in the Void whose shape may not be described, the young land floating like oil, Ame-no-minaka-nushi and the two Musubi in the Plain of High Heaven, the cloud with no place of attachment for its root, and the floating oil; the paired generations Uhiji-ni and Suhiji-ni, Oho-to-nochi and Oho-to-mahe, Omo-taru and Kashiko-ne; Izanagi and Izanami as the seventh generation; the jewel-spear thrust down and groping about to find the ocean; the brine coagulating into Onogoro; Onogoro made the pillar of the centre of the land; the circuit left and right; the woman speaking first and being told it was unlucky; the second circuit; the exchange about the source-places of the body; Ahaji reckoned as the placenta and taken no pleasure in; and the islands of Oho-yamato, Iyo-no-futana, Tsukushi, Oki and Sado
scholarship: Aston reports Motoori Norinaga's and Hirata Atsutane's judgement that the opening is a Chinese rationalistic essay awkwardly prefixed to genuine Japanese tradition, and Motoori's point that the connecting word 'hence' is meaningless where it stands. He judges the variant quotations a somewhat later addition indicating a large lost literature, and appends the Kiujiki scheme as further evidence of the confusion of the traditions
translation: Aston's English from the classical Chinese of the original
framing: NAMED IN THE HISTORICAL CONTEXT: a court chronicle written to establish an imperial genealogy descending from the sun goddess, in a Chinese form adopted as part of state-building; and a translation made in 1896 for a British learned society while that genealogy was live political material in Japan
uncertainty: LOW on the English. Aston's name etymologies are his own and he hedges several of them explicitly, including Izanagi and Izanami, which he suspects may be folk etymology
notes: The Kojiki is not used and no material from it is imported; where the two differ, only the Nihongi is followed. The scan is a Google digitisation with poor character recognition and mangled Japanese characters; every quoted phrase was checked against surrounding lines

title: The Birds
author: Aristophanes; anonymous English prose translation
date: produced at Athens 414 BCE; the translation is a late-nineteenth-century prose version, translator not named in the copy used
location: the parabasis, Greek lines 685-703, with the chorus's continuing address on the services of birds
type: PRIMARY / HISTORICAL SOURCE in translation
use: the address to mortals as creatures of clay whose life is darkness; the promise to teach the origin of the gods, the rivers, Erebos and Chaos, and the jibe at Prodicus; Chaos, Night, dark Erebos and deep Tartarus at the beginning with Earth, air and heaven non-existent; black-winged Night laying a germless egg in the bosom of the infinite deeps of Erebos; Eros springing from it after the revolution of long ages with glittering golden wings; his mating in Tartarus with dark Chaos and the hatching of the birds as the first race to see the light; the Immortals not existing until Eros had brought together the ingredients of the world; Heaven, Ocean, Earth and the blessed gods arising from that marriage; the claim of priority over Olympus; wings and the assistance of lovers, with the quail, waterfowl, goose and cock; the crane signalling sowing, the hanging-up of the tiller and Orestes' tunic; the kite and the shearing; the swallow and the selling of the winter tunic; and the claim to be Ammon, Delphi and Dodona
scholarship: Aristophanes is the earliest surviving witness to the Greek cosmic egg, centuries earlier than Damascius and the other late sources for Orphic theogony. How closely his lines track an actual Orphic poem is disputed and is not settled here
translation: Anonymous English prose. THE TRANSLATOR IS NOT NAMED IN THE FILE and none is asserted
framing: NAMED IN THE STORY AND THE SOURCE NOTE: this is a comedy, and the cosmogony is spoken by a chorus of birds arguing that they should be worshipped instead of the gods. It is a parody, and it is presented as one
uncertainty: MEDIUM on the relation between the parody and its target. LOW on the English quoted. The retelling gives what the comedy says, in the comedy's voice, and does not present it as Orphic doctrine
notes: THIS STORY REPLACED AN INTERNAL DUPLICATE — correction C-9. The comic material around the cosmogony is deliberately retained; removing it to leave a bare cosmology would misrepresent the source

title: The Hymns of the Rigveda, volume IV (Books IX and X)
author: anonymous Vedic poet, the hymn ascribed by tradition to Hiraṇyagarbha son of Prajāpati; trans. Ralph T. H. Griffith
date: hymn composed in the latest stratum of the Ṛgveda; Griffith's four-volume translation published 1889-1892
location: Book X, hymn CXXI, verses 1-10, with Griffith's headnote and his notes on verses 1, 3, 4, 7, 8 and 10
type: PRIMARY / HISTORICAL SOURCE in translation
use: Hiraṇyagarbha rising in the beginning as born only lord of all created beings and holding up earth and heaven; the refrain 'What god shall we adore with our oblation?'; the giving of vital breath, power and vigour and the gods' acknowledgement of his commandments; 'whose shade is death, whose lustre makes immortal'; sole rule over the moving world that breathes and slumbers, and lordship of biped and quadruped; the snow-covered mountains, the sea and Rasā, 'his arms are these'; the heavens made strong and the earth steadfast, light's realm and the sky-vault supported, mid-air measured; the two embattled armies trembling and looking to him under the risen sun; the mighty waters coming containing the universal germ and producing Agni, whence the gods' one spirit; his surveying the floods containing productive force and generating Worship, and being god of gods with none beside him; the plea that he never harm us; and the tenth verse naming Prajāpati and asking for store of riches
scholarship: Griffith's headnote states that Ka, 'who', was applied as a name to Prajāpati and others 'from a forced interpretation of the interrogative pronoun which occurs in the refrain', and records that some translators render the refrain as 'Worship we Ka the god'. He glosses hiraṇyagarbha as the gold-germ and quotes Wallis calling it the nearest approach in the Ṛgveda to the later conception of Brahmā
translation: Griffith's English verse from the Sanskrit
framing: A Victorian Indologist's translation made in Benares with Sāyaṇa's commentary; Griffith prints competing readings where the sense is disputed
uncertainty: LOW on the English quoted. The status of verse 10 as a later addition is scholarship and not stated by Griffith, and is labelled as such in the claim ledger
notes: Third hymn used from Griffith volume IV, after X.90 in S14 and X.129 at the close of S03. The scan has no title page; identity established by content and recorded in the source register. This story sits in the part called From an Egg although garbha means germ or embryo rather than egg; the difference is stated in the source note and the literal egg of the later Brāhmaṇa literature is not told here

title: Oceanic Mythology (The Mythology of All Races, vol. IX)
author: Roland B. Dixon, compiling from collections he cites by footnote number without naming reciters or recorders
date: Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916
location: ch. I, 'Myths of Origins and the Deluge', pp. 11-13 for the two Society Islands versions, and p. 20 for the egg fragment; p. 11 for the equivalence of Ta'aroa, Tanaoa, Tangaroa, Tangaloa and Kanaloa
type: SCHOLARSHIP quoting recorded chants; no narrator or collector named
use: the chant from 'He existed. Taaroa was his name' through the four negations, 'Taaroa calls, but nothing answers', 'Existing alone, he became the universe', the identifications with root, rocks, sands, light, the within, the germ, the support, endurance and wisdom, the raising of Havai'i as a body or shell, the imperatives to the foundations rocks and sands, 'They do not unite', the stretching of the seven heavens and the ceasing of ignorance, darkness, immobility and the period of messengers, 'It is the time of the speaker', and the completion; the second version with Ta'aroa embracing the rock, the heralds of day soliciting a soul, 'It is done', and Ra'i-tubu looking up, down and into the abyss so that each region received the power to bring forth; and the one-sentence fragment that Ta'aroa existed in an egg in darkness from which he later burst forth
scholarship: Dixon classifies Pacific origin-myths by type — evolutionary, creative — in the comparative manner of 1916, and notes the region-wide equivalence of the god's name while recording that his rank differs between island groups
translation: English as Dixon prints it; the underlying collectors are not named in the passage
framing: NAMED IN THE HISTORICAL CONTEXT: Society Islands material was recorded chiefly by London Missionary Society personnel during and after the dismantling of the traditional religion from 1797. Dixon is at a further remove, a Boston comparativist working from other people's collections
uncertainty: HIGH on attribution — no reciter and no recorder is named anywhere in the passage. LOW on the wording quoted, which is Dixon's printed text
notes: Second use of Dixon's volume IX, after the Māori genealogy in S05; the two are different island groups with different cosmological plans, and the story says so. 'Hawaii' in the chant is Havai'i, the old name of Ra'iātea, not the Hawaiian Islands — an identification recorded as scholarship because Dixon prints the name without comment

title: Development of Religion and Thought in Ancient Egypt
author: James Henry Breasted, translating the Memphite theology from British Museum Stela No. 797
date: the stone inscribed under Shabaka c. 700 BCE, copying an older papyrus; Breasted's book 1912
location: ch. II, 'The Origins', pp. 43-47, quoting the stela ll. 48-61; Breasted's footnote on the stone's history and the earlier copies by Sharpe and by Bryant and Read
type: PRIMARY / HISTORICAL SOURCE in translation, embedded in SCHOLARSHIP
use: Ptah the master craftsman and his Memphite ennead of a primeval Ptah and eight emanations; the borrowing of the ennead from Heliopolis; 'he is the heart and tongue of the ennead' and the identification of that heart and tongue with Atum; the Egyptian use of 'heart' for mind and the absence of a word for mind; the power of mind and tongue proceeding from Ptah and controlling all gods, men, animals and reptiles; the eyes, ears and nose transmitting to the heart, the heart bringing forth every issue and the tongue repeating its thought; the fashioning of all gods including Atum and his ennead; every divine word coming into existence by the thought of the heart and the commandment of the tongue; the making of the kas and the qualities, all food and offerings, that which is loved and hated, life to the peaceful and death to the guilty; the making of every work and handicraft, the going of the feet and the movement of every limb; Atum's statement concerning Ptah-Tatenen; Thoth perceiving his strength greater than all gods; 'Then Ptah was satisfied'; the making of cities and settling of nomes, the installing of gods in holy places, the likenesses of their bodies and the gods entering into bodies of every wood, stone and metal; and the summoning of the gods to the storehouse of Ptah-Tatenen
scholarship: Breasted's footnote gives the stone's history: used as a nether millstone, acquired by the British Museum in 1805, copied by Sharpe with the lines numbered backwards, copied again by Bryant and Read in 1901 still backwards, and corrected by Breasted himself in a facsimile in the Zeitschrift für ägyptische Sprache. He also asks whether the document is the primeval germ of the Alexandrian Logos, and states that the world Ptah made was merely the Egyptian Nile valley
translation: Breasted's English from the Egyptian
framing: NAMED IN THE SOURCE NOTE AND HISTORICAL CONTEXT: Breasted dates the underlying composition to the Pyramid Age and presents it as the earliest philosophical system in the world. The stone is Shabaka's, c. 700 BCE, and whether the text it copies is genuinely Old Kingdom or an archaising composition of that period has been argued since. This book gives his translation and does not repeat his dating
uncertainty: HIGH on date. MEDIUM on wording in the abraded passages, by Breasted's own warning that the signs are very faint and reading excessively difficult. He also flags the verb rendered 'thinking' as questionable and notes that heart and tongue share a gender so the pronoun may refer to either
notes: Second use of Breasted after S01. The two stories are the rival Heliopolitan and Memphite cosmogonies, which the Egyptians never reconciled and which this book presents as answers to each other

title: Latin-American Mythology (The Mythology of All Races, vol. XI) — the opening chapter of the Popol Vuh
author: anonymous K'iche' authors, 16th century; copied and translated into Spanish by Francisco Ximénez c. 1701; K'iche' text and French translation published by Charles Étienne Brasseur de Bourbourg, 1861; English by Hartley Burr Alexander
date: K'iche' manuscript mid-16th century; Brasseur 1861; Alexander 1920
location: Alexander, ch. IV, 'Central America', pp. 160-162, quoting the first chapter of the Popol Vuh entire
type: PRIMARY / HISTORICAL SOURCE at three removes of translation
use: the list of absences — no man, animal, bird, fish, wood, stone, bog, ravine, vegetation or marsh, only the sky; the face of the earth not yet to be seen; nothing formed into a body, nothing joined to another thing, naught poised, not a rustle nor a sound, naught standing upright; immobility and silence in the darkness and the night; Tepeu the Lord and Gucumatz the Plumed Serpent alone upon the waters like a growing light; their envelopment in green and azure whence the name; the Heart of the Sky naming himself; the word coming to them in the shadows and speaking with them; their consulting and joining of words and counsels; light coming while they consulted; Hurakan and his three signs, the Lightning, the Streak of Lightning and the Thunderbolt; the council on seed, light and the sustainer of all; the order to the waters to retire, with the stated reason that they will receive neither glory nor honour until sentient human beings exist; 'Earth, they said, and immediately it was formed'; the formation like fog or cloud and the mountains appearing like great lobsters, instantly grown with cypress and pine; Gucumatz's welcome to the Heart of the Sky by four names; the reply that what they have created will have its end; the dividing of the waters and the streams running serpentine among the mountains; and the closing description of those who first made fruitful the heaven and the earth while suspended in the midst of the waters
scholarship: Alexander introduces the passage as the first chapter of the Quiché Genesis and comments on it in the comparative idiom of 1920; his interpretation is not adopted
translation: Alexander's English from Brasseur's French. THE CHAIN WAS VERIFIED: Brasseur's 1861 volume is held for this edition and his French at the Hurakan passage was compared against Alexander's English and corresponds exactly
framing: NAMED IN THE HISTORICAL CONTEXT: a text written in the Roman alphabet introduced by the friars, within a generation of the conquest; copied by a Dominican; published by an editor who also wrote about Atlantis; and translated for an American comparative series
