BOUNDARY: the making of human beings from mud, wood and finally maize is not told here — Vâliçe has published that portion for young readers in another series, and this book takes the cosmogony only

title: History of the Incas
author: Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa, by order of Viceroy Francisco de Toledo; trans. Sir Clements Markham
date: written at Cuzco, 1572; Markham's translation for the Hakluyt Society, Cambridge, 1907
location: ch. VII, 'Fable of the second age, and creation of the barbarous Indians according to their account'; with Sarmiento's statement of commission and method at the opening of ch. VI, and Markham's footnotes on unu pachacuti and on Taguapaca
type: PRIMARY / HISTORICAL SOURCE — a colonial chronicle recording Andean tradition from Inca informants
use: the flood called unu pachacuti; the three men preserved, one named Taguapaca; the decision to people the land a second time and to make it more perfect by creating luminaries; the great lake in the Collao and the island Titicaca, the rock of lead; the order that sun, moon and stars come forth, 'and it was so'; the moon created brighter than the sun, the sun's jealousy and the handful of ashes; Taguapaca's disobedience, his binding hand and foot, his launching on a balsa, his blasphemy and threat of vengeance, and his disappearance down the drain of the lake; the sacred idol set up as a sign; the crossing to Tiahuanaco; the sculpturing and designing of all the nations on a great piece of stone; the servants charged to memorise the names of all tribes and of the valleys and provinces where they were to come forth; the three roads — the coastal range, the heights over the Andes, and Viracocha's own road between them; the shouted command to go forth and multiply and settle the land; the naming of every tribe and place; people coming forth from lakes, fountains, valleys, caves, trees, rocks and hills; and the variant account in which the creation was made at Titicaca, the first shapes being out of proportion and remade at the creator's own stature
scholarship: Sarmiento states that the history rests on attested proofs from the general testimony of the whole kingdom, old and young, Incas and tributary Indians. On completion it was read aloud in Quechua to an assembly of Inca elders and keepers of the knotted-cord records in Cuzco for certification
translation: Markham's English from the Spanish
framing: NAMED IN THE STORY, THE SOURCE NOTE AND THE HISTORICAL CONTEXT: the book was written by order of Viceroy Toledo as part of a programme to establish that the Incas had been usurpers and that Spanish rule was therefore legitimate. It was written in the year Toledo had the last Inca ruler beheaded at Cuzco
uncertainty: MEDIUM on the flood, by the translator's own warning that unu pachacuti was probably coined by priests after leading questions about a universal deluge. LOW on the wording quoted
notes: Chapter VI, the first creation and its destruction, is told separately as S27 in the part of this book called From Many Attempts; the two chapters are consecutive in the source and are not the same story. Markham collects the variant names of Taguapaca from Cieza de León and Yamqui Pachacuti and concludes nothing more can be recovered
workAuthor: Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa; trans. Sir Clements Markham

title: The Yoruba-Speaking Peoples of the Slave Coast of West Africa
author: A. B. Ellis, Colonel, 1st West India Regiment
date: London: Chapman and Hall, 1894
location: ch. III, 'Chief Gods', the sections on (1) Olorun, (2) Obatala and (3) Odudua; with the migration tradition in the later chapter, cited in the source note but not retold
type: HISTORICAL SOURCE — COLONIAL-ERA ETHNOGRAPHY recording Yoruba tradition; no narrator named
use: Olorun as Owner of the Sky, maker of Obatala, who handed over the management of the firmament and the world and retired to rest; his lack of priests, symbols, images and temples and his survival in greetings and exclamations; Obatala as Lord of the White Cloth and the whiteness of his temples, images and followers; Odudua as the Black One, chief goddess, always shown seated nursing a child, coeval with Olorun and not made by him; the identification of the pair as Heaven and Earth; the priests' image of two large cut calabashes which once shut can never be opened, and the two whitened saucer-calabashes in the temples with the rim as the horizon; the myth of the two shut in darkness in a large closed calabash, he above and she below, for many days, cramped, hungry and uncomfortable; her complaint and blame, the violent quarrel, his tearing out her eyes because she would not bridle her tongue, and her curse that he should eat nothing but snails, whence the snail offerings; Ellis's observation that the myth never restores her sight yet no native regards her as blind; the disputed myth of Obatala making the first man and woman from clay, with the titles Owner of the Best Clay and the Orisha Who Kneads Clay; the agreement that he forms the child in the womb; and the minority view that the two are one androgynous divinity symbolised by a one-armed, one-legged figure with a tail ending in a sphere
scholarship: Ellis gives etymologies and marks the disputed ones, prints variants without choosing, distinguishes common belief from minority view, and notes where a myth fails to follow through
translation: Ellis's English; no Yoruba text is printed
framing: NAMED IN THE HISTORICAL CONTEXT: an officer of the 1st West India Regiment writing in 1894, during the British extension of authority across Yorubaland, in the racial idiom of his decade, with a recurring interest in whether religious practice is trickery
uncertainty: HIGH on attribution — every account is credited only to 'the priests', 'some natives' or 'other natives', with no informant, place or date. LOW on the wording, which was checked against the scan
notes: THE PLANNED STORY IS NOT IN THIS SOURCE — correction C-12. The chain, the snail shell of sand and the five-toed hen come from later works not obtainable in public domain; Ellis's nearest equivalent, the palm-nut and the scratching fowl, belongs to his migration tradition and is described in the source note rather than told. Material in the chapter concerning albinism, congenital disability and a divination cylinder is not used

title: African Mythology (The Mythology of All Races, vol. VII)
author: Alice Werner, reporting the fieldwork of Emil Torday among the Bushongo of the Kasai
date: Boston: Marshall Jones, 1925; Torday's fieldwork 1907-09
location: the chapter on myths of origins, in the section on creation legends
type: SCHOLARSHIP reporting an ethnographer's field record; no narrator named
use: Bumba described as a gigantic white being in human form, existing alone in a universe where there was nothing but water; the severe internal pains and the vomiting up of the sun, moon and stars, giving light to the world; the sun's rays drying the water so that sandbanks appeared, with no life anywhere; the production in the same manner of the living creatures — leopard, crested eagle, crocodile, a small fish parent of all fish, tortoise, the lightning described as a beast like a black leopard, white heron, beetle and goat; the subsequent production of men; the animals undertaking to people the world, with the goat producing horned beasts, the beetle insects, the crocodile serpents and the iguana, and the white heron all birds except the kite; Bumba's three sons, the first producing white ants and dying in the effort, the second a plant from which all vegetable life sprang, and the third producing only the kite; and Werner's statement that why the kite should be set apart is not explained
scholarship: Werner states she has met no parallel to this legend elsewhere in Africa; she raises the resemblance to Genesis I herself and defends the material's independence on the grounds that the Bushongo were untouched by missionary influence and that Torday was unusually independent of interpreters. She also notes that Bumba is First Ancestor as well as Creator and that the reigning chiefs preserve every link of descent from him
translation: Werner's English, reporting Torday
framing: NAMED IN THE HISTORICAL CONTEXT: collected in the Kasai in 1907-09, during and immediately after the Congo Free State, in a kingdom whose rising had been put down in 1904; and gathered as part of a museum-collecting expedition
uncertainty: MEDIUM. Werner's claim that the Bushongo were entirely untouched by missionary influence is a strong one for the Kasai at that date and is questioned in the source note. Her count of the creatures — eight stated, nine listed — is left uncorrected because the error cannot be located
notes: The plan called this people Bakuba; Kuba is the standard modern name of the kingdom and Bushoong of the group. No Bushongo narrator is named anywhere in the source

title: Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns and Homerica — Works and Days
author: Hesiod; trans. Hugh G. Evelyn-White
date: composed c. 700 BCE; translation Loeb Classical Library, 1914
location: Works and Days ll. 106-201, with ll. 202-211 for the hawk and the nightingale
type: PRIMARY / HISTORICAL SOURCE in translation
use: the promise to tell another tale of how gods and mortal men sprang from one source; the golden race made under Cronos, free from toil and grief, dying as if overcome with sleep, fed by the earth unforced, and becoming pure spirits clothed in mist who watch judgements and give wealth; the silver race, less noble by far, the child reared a hundred years as an utter simpleton, their brief and sorrowful maturity, their refusal to sacrifice, Zeus putting them away, and their becoming blessed spirits of the underworld of second rank; the brazen race sprung from ash-trees, terrible and strong, eating no bread, hard as adamant, with bronze armour, houses and implements and no black iron, destroyed by their own hands and leaving no name; the fourth race of hero demi-gods, nobler and more righteous, destroyed in part at seven-gated Thebe over the flocks of Oedipus and at Troy for Helen, the rest settled by Zeus in the islands of the blessed where the earth bears fruit thrice a year under the released Cronos; and the fifth race of iron, Hesiod's wish to have been born at another time, the labour and sorrow, the good mingled with the evils, the sign of grey hair at birth, the catalogue of failing bonds, the praise of evil-doers, the departure of Aidos and Nemesis in white robes, and the absence of help against evil; then the fable for princes of the hawk and the nightingale
scholarship: The insertion of the heroes between bronze and iron interrupts a scheme of metallic decline and is generally read as Hesiod combining an inherited myth of decline with a heroic age his audience knew from epic
translation: Evelyn-White's English, Loeb 1914, public domain
framing: None colonial. The poem is a partisan document in a family inheritance dispute and an attack on the magistrates who decided it, and the historical context says so
uncertainty: LOW on the English. The exact sense of the line rendered 'grey hair on the temples at their birth' is debated, though the image is not
notes: Second Hesiod entry, from a different poem than S02. Aidos and Nemesis are left untranslated because no single English word carries either; the source note explains both

title: History of the Incas
author: Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa, by order of Viceroy Francisco de Toledo; trans. Sir Clements Markham
date: written at Cuzco, 1572; Markham's translation for the Hakluyt Society, Cambridge, 1907
location: ch. VI, the first creation and its destruction; Markham's long footnote on the derivations of Viracocha; Sarmiento's own remarks fitting the Andean flood to the biblical one
type: PRIMARY / HISTORICAL SOURCE — a colonial chronicle recording Andean tradition from Inca informants
use: the being called Viracocha existing before this world was created; his creation of a dark world without sun, moon or stars and the resulting name Viracocha Pachayachachi, Creator of all things; the race of giants of disproportioned greatness, painted and sculptured, made to see whether it would be well to make real men of that size; the making of men in his own likeness, living in darkness; the order to live without quarrelling and to know and serve him; the single precept to be kept on pain of being confounded, and the statement that it is not mentioned what it was; the keeping of it for some time; the arising of pride and covetousness and the transgression; the confounding and cursing; the turning of some into stones, others into other things, the swallowing of some by the earth and others by the sea; the general flood called unu pachacuti, water that overturns the land, raining sixty days and nights and drowning all created things; the surviving vestiges of those turned into stones as a memorial and an example to posterity in the edifices of Pucara, sixty leagues from Cuzco; and Sarmiento's note that other nations say a few were saved and that each nation has its own fable
scholarship: Markham collects the competing derivations of Viracocha from Garcilasso, Cieza de León, Acosta, Montesinos, Molina, Betanzos and an anonymous Jesuit without choosing, and glosses Pachayachachi as Teacher of the Universe. He warns in the following chapter that unu pachacuti was probably coined by priests after leading questions about a universal deluge
translation: Markham's English from the Spanish
framing: NAMED IN THE HISTORICAL CONTEXT: written by order of Viceroy Toledo as part of a programme to establish the Incas as usurpers; and containing Sarmiento's own accommodation of the Andean flood to the biblical one, with an Atlantic land connection, so that recording it should not require setting aside the Scriptures
uncertainty: MEDIUM on the flood, by the translator's own warning. LOW on the wording quoted. The content of the broken precept is stated by the source itself to be unknown
notes: Chapter VII, the second creation, is told separately earlier in this book. The two chapters are consecutive in the source and describe two different worlds
workAuthor: Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa; trans. Sir Clements Markham

title: Latin-American Mythology (The Mythology of All Races, vol. XI) — the Mixtec cosmogony
author: narrated by Fray Gregorio García, early 17th century; quoted and summarised by Hartley Burr Alexander
date: García early 1600s; Alexander, Boston: Marshall Jones, 1920
location: Alexander, ch. III, 'Mexico (Continued)', section I 'Cosmogony', where he quotes García's opening sentence and summarises the narrative in four numbered episodes; and the following paragraph on the Zapotec Coqui-Xee, Piye-Tao, Cozaana and Huichaana
type: SCHOLARSHIP quoting a colonial document that records Mixtec tradition
use: the opening sentence quoted in full — the year and day of obscurity and darkness when there were as yet no days nor years, the world a chaos sunk in darkness, the earth covered with water on which scum and slime floated; the Deer-God and Deer-Goddess, also known as the Puma-Snake and the Jaguar-Snake; their magical raising of a cliff above the abyss of waters; the axe placed edge upward on its summit, upon which the heavens rested; the Place-where-the-Heavens-stood and their dwelling there many centuries; their two sons, Wind-of-the-Nine-Serpents and Wind-of-the-Nine-Caves, able to transform into eagles and serpents and to pass through solid bodies; their inauguration of sacrifice and penance and the cultivation of flowers and fruits; their prayer to their ancestral gods that the light appear, that the water be separated from the earth and that the dry land be freed from its covering; the peopling of the earth; and the flood that destroyed the First People, after which the world was restored by the Creator of all Things; and, from the Zapotec paragraph Alexander links to it, Coqui-Xee or Coqui-Cilla, Lord of the Beginning, 'the creator of all things and was himself uncreated'; his second name Piye-Tao, the Great Wind; Seler's reading of him as a spirit of the beginning in the sense of dawn, the east and the rising sun; the statement that he is merely the principle or essence of deity without reference to the act of creating; and the primeval pair Cozaana, Maker of all Beasts, and Huichaana, Maker of Men and Fishes, given as the Zapotec equivalents of the Mixtec Deer-God and Deer-Goddess
scholarship: Alexander observes that the opening's description of the void by negation resembles Genesis and the Babylonian cosmogony, and explains the device as characteristic of an early stage of human thought — the evolutionary anthropology of 1920, quoted and not adopted. His identifications of the deer as an emblem of fecundity, of the Puma-Snake and Jaguar-Snake as day-sky and night-vault, and of the two boys as demiurgic twins are his own and are not used
translation: Alexander's English; the opening sentence is his quotation of García
framing: NAMED IN THE HISTORICAL CONTEXT: a Dominican collecting American origin traditions in part to test theories about where the peoples of the New World had come from — a purpose unlike the tradition's own
uncertainty: MEDIUM. Only the opening sentence is quotation; the rest is Alexander's summary of García's account, so the wording of the narrative is at two removes and no phrasing beyond the first sentence should be treated as the source's own
notes: THIS STORY REPLACED AN INTERNAL DUPLICATE — correction C-10. The Mixtec are a distinct people from the Mexica, with their own language, dynasties and codices; the two Mesoamerican entries in this book come from different peoples and different documents

title: Oceanic Mythology (The Mythology of All Races, vol. IX)
author: Roland B. Dixon, compiling from collections cited by footnote number without naming reciters or recorders
date: Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916
location: ch. I, 'Myths of Origins and the Deluge', pp. 18-19, in the section on the creative type
type: SCHOLARSHIP reporting collected tradition; no narrator named
use: the Samoan account — Tangaloa in the high heavens seeing a stone floating in the boundless sea, bringing it up, shaping it into human form, inspiring it with life and taking it to wife; her bearing him a bird; his sending the bird down and casting a great rock into the sea to serve it for a home; the bird's return complaining of the shadeless character of the land; the casting down of a vine which grew and gave shadow; Tangaloa in anger sending worms which fed on the vines and killed them; and man later made from the worms or maggots developed from the rotting vines. And the Tongan account — Tama-pouli-alamafoa the King of Heaven, Tangaloa-eiki the Celestial Chief, Tangaloa-tufuga the Celestial Artisan and Tangaloa-atu-logologo the Celestial Messenger; the messenger sent down on a bird and finding only a sandbank; the instruction to wait seven days and look again; the land found risen; the further instruction to wait and look once more; his complaint that there was nowhere to rest; the instruction to ask the artificer to cast down chips and shavings from his work; the rising of the island of Eua; his report of a great land with no plant or tree; and the seed given by the divine chief, which grew into a great vine covering all the land
scholarship: Dixon identifies the constant features of this type as a pre-existing world of the gods above, a universal sea below, something cast down from one into the other from which the world is made, and a bird who is messenger or offspring of the sky-deity. His division of Pacific origin-myths into evolutionary and creative types is a scheme of his period and is not adopted
translation: English as Dixon prints it; the underlying collectors are not named in the passage
framing: NAMED IN THE HISTORICAL CONTEXT: Pacific material recorded in the nineteenth century by missionaries and residents after the London Missionary Society reached Tonga in 1797 and Samoa in 1830, published in collections, and compiled at a distance in Massachusetts in 1916
uncertainty: HIGH on attribution — no reciter, recorder, place or date is given for either account. LOW on the wording, which is Dixon's printed text
notes: THIS STORY REPLACED A PLANNED SLAVIC ENTRY THAT ITS SOURCE DOES NOT CONTAIN — correction C-13. Third and final use of Dixon in this book, after S05 (Māori) and S20 (Society Islands); the three are different archipelagos and share no material. The source gives no reason for Tangaloa's anger and none is supplied

title: The Elder Eddas of Saemund Sigfusson — Vǫluspá
author: anonymous Old Norse poem; trans. Benjamin Thorpe
date: poem of disputed age, preserved in the Codex Regius of c. 1270; Thorpe's translation 1866, in the Norrœna Society edition
location: Vǫluspá 56-65, with 7-8 for the golden tables
type: PRIMARY / HISTORICAL SOURCE in translation
use: the sun darkening, the earth sinking in ocean, the stars falling, fire assailing the all-nourishing tree and playing against heaven; the seeress seeing earth rise a second time, beauteously green, with waterfalls descending and an eagle over the fell catching fish; the Æsir meeting on Ida's plain to speak of the earth-encircler and recall their deeds and the supreme god's ancient lore; the wondrous golden tables found again in the grass, which the ruler of the gods had possessed in days of old; the unsown fields bringing forth, all evil amended, and the coming of Baldr, with Höðr and Baldr inhabiting Hropt's dwellings; the refrain 'Understand ye yet, or what?'; Hœnir choosing his lot and the two brothers' sons inhabiting Vindheim; the hall brighter than the sun, decked with gold, at Gimlé, where righteous people dwell in everlasting happiness; the coming of the mighty one from above to the great judgment, pronouncing dooms, allaying strifes and establishing a holy peace; and the dark dragon Níðhǫggr flying from Niðafjöll over the plain bearing a corpse on his wings, followed by the seeress's descent
scholarship: The closing stanzas' resemblance to Christian eschatology — Gimlé, the mighty one from above, the sinless renewed world — has been argued over since the poem entered scholarship; three positions are set out in the source note and none is adopted
translation: Thorpe's English from the Old Norse
framing: NAMED IN THE SOURCE NOTE AND HISTORICAL CONTEXT: written down in Christian Iceland some two and a half centuries after the conversion, and heavily enlisted since the nineteenth century by nationalist and later by extremist movements; the version given is the thirteenth-century Icelandic one
uncertainty: HIGH on the poem's date and on the pagan or Christian character of the closing stanzas. LOW on the English quoted. Thorpe's numbering skips stanza 63 and nothing has been supplied
notes: Second and final use of the Elder Edda, after S12. The file is named for Bellows and is Thorpe — correction C-2. Some editors move or discount the final stanza on the grounds that a renewal ought not to end with a corpse-eating dragon; Thorpe prints it last and this book keeps it there
